While the filters above punish individual users, escalation watches the whole chat:
if many different users cause violations in a short time (a spam wave), a Twitch chat mode
like slow mode or follower-only is activated automatically to protect the entire chat.
The mode is chosen based on the dominant spam pattern of the wave:
Emote spam → slow > follow > sub (emote-only is excluded — it would legalize the spam)
Fresh accounts / message flooding → follow > sub > slow (locks out throwaway accounts entirely)
Caps/character spam → emote-only > slow > follow > sub (makes text spam impossible)
Only modes enabled below can be chosen — disabled modes fall through to the next preference.
Step up the response if a spam wave cont:
Step up the response if a spam wave continues despite an active chat mode.
When the violation count is reached AGAIN while a mode is already running, the next suitable
mode from the preference list is activated on top of it.
(Example emote wave: 1st trigger = slow mode; spam continues, 2nd trigger = follower-only is added)
Disabled: repeated triggers only extend the duration of the already active mode.
Always layer slow mode on top of whichev:
Always layer slow mode on top of whichever mode was auto-selected.
(Example: a fresh-account wave selects follower-only → slow mode is switched on as well,
so even users who pass the follow check can only post slowly)
Requires 'SlowMode Enabled'. Has no effect when slow mode itself is the chosen mode.
Allow escalation to use Twitch slow mode:
Allow escalation to use Twitch slow mode.
Every user must wait between their own messages — spam gets massively throttled,
but nobody is locked out of chat. The gentlest mode and therefore the first choice
for emote waves and mixed spam patterns.
Allow escalation to use follower-only mo:
Allow escalation to use follower-only mode.
Only users following the channel for at least 'Follow Age' can chat.
First choice against fresh-account waves and coordinated message flooding (bot attacks),
because throwaway accounts typically don't follow — the whole wave is locked out at once
while your regular viewers keep chatting normally.
Allow escalation to use emote-only mode.
Only Twitch emotes can be posted — text messages become impossible, which stops
caps and character floods completely. First choice for caps waves,
but drastic for normal chatters: if it's too harsh for your community, leave it disabled
and slow mode takes over as the next preference.
Never chosen for emote spam or flood waves.

Remember each link's scan result for a w:
Remember each link's scan result for a while, so the same link posted again is answered from memory instead of costing another API call.
This is what keeps a raid affordable: thirty accounts pasting one link is one scan, not thirty. Every one of those messages is still deleted and still gets its notification — only the lookup is skipped.
Turn this off only if you want every single post re-scanned live.
How long a remembered scan result stays:
How long a remembered scan result stays usable before the link is scanned again.
Shorter means a site that gets compromised is re-checked sooner; longer means fewer API calls.
60 minutes is a good balance — a raid arrives inside a few minutes, so even a short window catches it, while an hour keeps a busy chat well inside the daily quota.
How many links in a single message Twitc:
How many links in a single message TwitchSentry will scan before it stops and ignores the rest.
Every scan costs one call against your API quota (VirusTotal's free tier allows 4 per minute and 500 per day), and a link the scanner has never seen before takes around 20 seconds to come back.
Without a cap, one message pasted full of links can spend the whole day's quota and hold up moderation while it works through them.
3 is plenty for real conversation. Raise it only if you genuinely expect people to post several links at once.
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan mess:
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan messages so they cannot be clicked — "example.com" is posted as "example[.]com".
The bot is a moderator, so nothing filters what it says. Repeating a malicious link back into chat, right after deleting the message that carried it, hands it out again from an account viewers trust.
Turn this off only if you would rather the links stayed clickable.

How many letters a message needs before:
How many letters a message needs before the caps-percentage check bothers looking at it.

How many times the exact same character:
How many times the exact same character has to repeat in a row to count as character spam.

Sliding time window in which a user's me:
Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted.

Maximum number of messages a user may send within the window.

Sliding time window in which repeated me:
Sliding time window in which repeated messages are compared.

Number of identical or similar messages:
Number of identical or similar messages (including the current one) within the window
required to trigger a score hit.
(Example: 3 = posting the same content a 3rd time triggers)
Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate check.
Short messages like 'gg' or 'lol' are ignored — repeated short messages are still caught by the velocity check.
How many DIFFERENT users must be among t:
How many DIFFERENT users must be among the counted violations before escalation may trigger.
This is what separates a spam wave from one annoying person: a single spammer is handled
by delete/timeout and should never put the whole chat into slow mode.
(Example: 2 = at least two different users must be involved, no matter how many violations one user racks up)
Sliding time window in which filtered vi:
Sliding time window in which filtered violations are counted toward escalation.
Violations older than this no longer count — so 'Violation Count' must be reached within this timespan.

Total number of filtered violations with:
Total number of filtered violations within the window required to trigger escalation.
Counts every violation the Message Filter acts on (caps, emotes, account age, flood), across all users.
Lower = reacts faster to small waves; higher = only reacts to sustained attacks.
(Example: 3 violations by 2 users within 60s = escalation triggers with default settings)
How long the activated chat mode stays o:
How long the activated chat mode stays on before it is lifted automatically.
Every renewed trigger during an active mode resets this timer to its full value,
so the protection stays up as long as the wave continues and ends on its own afterwards.
(Example: 300 = chat returns to normal 5 minutes after the last escalation trigger)
Seconds each user must wait between thei:
Seconds each user must wait between their own messages while slow mode is active.
This is Twitch's per-message delay — NOT how long the mode stays on (see 'Duration').
(Example: 10 = each user can post at most one message every 10 seconds)
Minimum follow age in minutes required t:
Minimum follow age in minutes required to chat while follower-only mode is active.
0 = following at all is enough. Higher values also lock out bots that follow
right before attacking.

How long the raid protection stays armed:
How long the raid protection stays armed after an incoming raid.

Only arm the protection for raids with a:
Only arm the protection for raids with at least this many viewers.

Sliding time window in which a user's me: Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted during the raid window.

Number of identical or similar messages from the same user within the window required to trigger.

Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate and swarm checks.

The floor: how many distinct users have:
The floor: how many distinct users have to post near-identical messages within the window. The share below can raise it, never lower it.
(Example: 5 = the 5th account posting the wave message is what makes it a coordinated swarm, provided the wording is on a spam list)
The second half of the bar, as a percent:
The second half of the bar, as a percentage of the viewers the raid arrived with. The check takes whichever is larger, this or the count above.
Three accounts posting the same line is most of a raid of four and nothing at all in a raid of nine hundred; a flat number cannot mean the same thing in both.
0 turns the share off and leaves the flat count. Ignored when Twitch sent no viewer count with the raid.
What a message adds to the score for mat:
What a message adds to the score for matching this channel's spam lists, on its own — whether or not anybody else posted it.
It is not enough alone: one spam-flavoured message is the Spam Filter's job. Alongside a swarm or a repeat it is what tips a raid into being acted on.
How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts wh: How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts when "Action On Violation" above is set to Timeout. Example: 600 = 10 minutes.
How many emotes a message needs to have:
How many emotes a message needs to have before the emote-percentage check even looks at it.
Messages with fewer emotes than this are always ignored by that check.
How long (in seconds) the escalation tim: How long (in seconds) the escalation timeout lasts. Example: 60 = 1 minute.
If a viewer goes this many hours without: If a viewer goes this many hours without another violation, their warning count resets back to zero — so a warning from weeks ago doesn't count against them forever.
How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by: How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by default when a moderator grants one. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
The longest permit anyone can hand out. A moderator who types a longer time in "!Permit @user 3000" gets this instead, and so does a default or self-permit duration set above it.
This is what stops a mistyped duration from switching moderation off for someone for hours. Capped at 86400 (24 hours) whatever you put here.

"!EndPermit" with no name ends every active permit at once.
Set the reward up on Twitch with \"Skip:
Set the reward up on Twitch with "Skip Reward Requests Queue" turned OFF. That is what lets TwitchSentry give the points back when a redemption cannot become a permit — the viewer already has one, or the feature is off. Point the reward's Streamer.bot trigger at this same Permit action.
How long (in seconds) a self-granted per: How long (in seconds) a self-granted permit lasts. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
How long (in hours) the learner keeps it:
How long (in hours) the learner keeps its downloaded list of common, everyday words (in many languages) before refreshing it. This list stops ordinary words like "the" or "und" from ever being suggested as spam.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = refreshes more often (rarely needed — this list barely changes).

How long (in hours) the learner keeps its downloaded list of valid domain endings (.com, .net, etc.) before refreshing it.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = refreshes more often (rarely needed).
How many DIFFERENT people need to have p:
How many DIFFERENT people need to have posted something before it can even become a suggestion.
This stops one repeat spammer from single-handedly teaching the learner a new rule — real spam campaigns usually involve more than one account.
The minimum \"confidence score\" somethi:
The minimum "confidence score" something needs before it's written down as a suggestion for you to review.
Confidence is a combined score based on how often it showed up, how many different messages and people it came from, and how spam-like the message around it looked.
The minimum confidence score a suggestio:
The minimum confidence score a suggestion needs to become "trusted" and be eligible for auto-promotion into spam.json.
Only matters if "Auto Promote Trusted Rules" above is turned on.
How many separate learner runs a suggest:
How many separate learner runs a suggestion has to keep reappearing in before it can be auto-promoted.
Makes sure it's a real, repeating pattern rather than a one-off fluke before it becomes an active rule.
The minimum number of times something ha:
The minimum number of times something has to show up (weighted) across recent violations before the learner even considers it.
This is just an early sanity check — it still has to clear the other requirements (how many messages, how many different people, and confidence) before actually becoming a suggestion.
The minimum number of separate violation:
The minimum number of separate violation-log entries something has to appear in before it can be suggested.
Stops a single, very repetitive spam message from teaching the learner a new rule all by itself.
Higher = more cautious/slower to react. Lower = reacts sooner, with less proof behind it.
The most single-word keyword suggestions:
The most single-word keyword suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run.
A safety cap so a single busy run can't flood your suggestions list.
The most two-word phrase suggestions the:
The most two-word phrase suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run.
Phrase suggestions tend to be more specific/precise than single-word keywords.
The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggest: The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggestions the learner is allowed to add or refresh in one run, based on spaced-out or disguised links it spotted.
How many of the most recent lines in vio:
How many of the most recent lines in violation-log.txt the learner reads through each time it looks for new patterns.
More lines = more history to learn from (usually more reliable results), but takes a little longer to process each run.
How much extra weight the message that j:
How much extra weight the message that just triggered this run gets, compared to older messages in the history.
Higher = the newest violation influences this run's results more strongly — but it still has to pass the same requirements as everything else before it can become a suggestion.
Controls how hard a word gets penalized:
Controls how hard a word gets penalized if it also shows up a lot in ordinary, non-violating chat (see "Clean-Chat Sample Rate" below).
Lower = stricter — everyday words that also appear in normal chat get suppressed more aggressively, which helps avoid false positives (like accidentally suggesting "google").
TwitchSentry saves roughly 1 out of ever:
TwitchSentry saves roughly 1 out of every N normal (non-violating) chat messages to clean-log.txt, to build up a sample of what everyday chat looks like — this feeds the Clean Penalty Divisor above.
Higher = samples less often and keeps the file smaller. Lower = builds the sample faster, but writes to disk more often.
The largest clean-log.txt is allowed to:
The largest clean-log.txt is allowed to grow (in kilobytes) before it's automatically trimmed down to just the most recent entries (see "History Lines" above).
Keeps this file from growing forever during long or very active streams.
How many separate learner runs a brand-n:
How many separate learner runs a brand-new suggestion has to keep appearing in before it's upgraded from "probation" to "trusted".
Higher = slower but safer. Lower = reacts faster, with less proof.
How many learner runs a pending suggesti:
How many learner runs a pending suggestion is allowed to go without reappearing before it's automatically removed from the suggestions list.
Gives suggestions some breathing room so a brief quiet spell doesn't wipe them out immediately.
How many of the most recent violation-lo: How many of the most recent violation-log entries are checked when deciding what still counts as "active" during cleanup.
How many times a rule or suggestion has:
How many times a rule or suggestion has to show up within that recent window to count as still active and be kept.
Higher = cleans up more aggressively. Lower = keeps rarely-used patterns around longer.
How strict Twitch's own AutoMod needs to:
How strict Twitch's own AutoMod needs to be before TwitchSentry acts on a held message. Twitch normally uses level 2 ("SmartDetection") as the baseline.
Goes from 1 to 4 — 4 is the strictest, but can start flagging (and then removing) messages you'd actually want to allow through.
IPQS rates every link on a scale from 0:
IPQS rates every link on a scale from 0 (totally safe) to 100 (certainly malicious). This is the minimum score at which TwitchSentry treats a link as a threat.
At 75, a link is considered suspicious (often a proxy, VPN exit node, or known bad actor).
IPQS's own guidance is 85 to outright block and 75 to flag for review — so 75 is the cautious, safer default.
Raise it toward 90 if you're seeing too many false alarms on your channel.
A lower, stricter version of the thresho:
A lower, stricter version of the threshold above, used only when IPQS also flags the domain as recently registered (i.e. a brand-new website).
Brand-new throwaway domains are a classic phishing trick — register one, use it once, then abandon it.
Since a new domain is inherently riskier, even a fraud score as low as 40 (normally considered "low risk") is enough to trigger a warning here.
Set this higher (e.g. 60-70) if you want to give new domains more benefit of the doubt.
How long (in seconds) the timeout lasts: How long (in seconds) the timeout lasts when a vote succeeds. Example: 1800 = 30 minutes.
How many different viewers need to vote: How many different viewers need to vote before the vote succeeds and action is taken.

How similar two messages must be to count as duplicates, from 0.0 to 1.0.

How similar two messages must be to count as duplicates, from 0.0 to 1.0.

Score added on a swarm hit.

What percentage of the message needs to:
What percentage of the message needs to be emotes before it counts as emote spam during a raid. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.65 = 65%).
Example: 0.65 = a message that's more than 65% emotes adds to the score.
What percentage of the message's letters:

Example: 0.65 = a message where more than 65% of its letters are capitals adds to the score.
Covered up by default, so the window is: Covered up by default, so the window is safe to have on screen. Click the eye to uncover a value, or paste a new one straight into the dots with Ctrl+V — you never have to uncover a field just to replace it.

If none appears, Windows is holding it back: look at Do Not Disturb (Focus Assist) and at Settings → System → Notifications, where Streamer.bot has to be allowed to send notifications.
The Link Filter has no page of its own,: The Link Filter has no page of its own, so its action is set on the Message Filter page, in the Link Filter card. It is one choice for three modules: the Message Filter, the Link Filter and the Spam Filter all act the way it is set there.
The other Message Filter checks deal wit: The other Message Filter checks deal with one viewer at a time. Escalation deals with the whole chat: when enough different people trip the filters inside the same window, a Twitch chat mode is switched on for everyone and lifted again on its own. Which mode is picked depends on what the wave looks like — the table at the bottom of the Escalation card shows exactly what would happen with the boxes as they are ticked right now.
Everything else on the Raid Protection p: Everything else on the Raid Protection page measures shape: how fast, how often, how many at once. None of that can tell a community arriving with its own catchphrase from a bot wave, because the two look identical from the outside. The wording is what separates them.
The same ladder the Message Filter uses,: The same ladder the Message Filter uses, running on the raid window instead of on ordinary chat. Which mode is picked depends on what the wave looks like; the table at the bottom of the Escalation card shows exactly what would happen with the boxes as they are ticked right now.

A block is not a ban. Banning leaves the follower on your list, while a block removes the follow and stops the account following again. It is also quiet: no mod-log entry to read through after a wave.
Blocking is invisible from the viewer's side, though: they simply cannot follow, and nobody tells them. That is why this ships on Report Only, and why every block is written to the Blocked Accounts list and can be lifted with !tsundo.
⚠ This is the setting most likely to hi: ⚠  This is the setting most likely to hit a real person. A viewer who made an account this morning to follow you looks exactly like a bot on every Follow Protection check — young, no picture, empty profile. The wave rule is what normally protects them, and Judge Single Follows Too removes it. Leave it off unless you are being followed by single accounts spread out over hours, and pair it with Report Only first.
A different type of bot than the one tha: A different type of bot than the one that drops one advert and leaves. This account chats with you: it asks how long you have been streaming, says your channel looks a little empty, mentions that a logo or a VTuber model would fix that, and only then tells you it sells exactly that. No single message it sends is an advert, so the advert rules cannot see it — this is still considered WIP so expect false flags.
The Spam Learner watches messages that g: The Spam Learner watches messages that get deleted, timed out, or banned, and tries to spot new spam words and phrases in them automatically. New finds start out as "suggestions" for you to review on the Suggestions tab, and only get added to the real, active rule list (spam.json) once they've proven themselves — either you approve them yourself, or (if Auto Promote Trusted Rules is on) the learner promotes them on its own once they've been seen often enough, from enough different people, to be trustworthy.
These are the actual, active spam rules: These are the actual, active spam rules TwitchSentry checks every message against — shared by every module. Add entries yourself, or let the Spam Learner suggest new ones for you to approve on the Suggestions tab (or have it auto-approve them, if "Auto Promote Trusted Rules" is turned on in the Learner settings).
New viewer-selling sites and bot wording: New viewer-selling sites and bot wording are published once, to TwitchSentry's spam feed on GitHub, and reach every install from there within a few hours. Each entry is added to the Known Patterns lists exactly once: delete one and it stays deleted. The feed only ever adds to the plain-text lists - custom patterns and voucher patterns stay yours alone. Wording you have found yourself can go the other way: share it, and once it holds up it reaches everyone else.
The four stages of the sales conversatio: The four stages of the sales conversation described on the Spam Scoring page. Plain text, one phrase per line, matched anywhere in a message and case-insensitively. None of these phrases does anything on its own — an account has to move through three of these stages in order and end on the offer. That is why the first stage's list may look completely harmless: it is meant to.
Twitch AutoMod is Twitch's own built-in: Twitch AutoMod is Twitch's own built-in filter — it automatically holds back messages that might be harmful or break chat rules, and normally waits for a moderator to manually approve or deny each one. This module lets TwitchSentry make that approve/deny decision automatically instead, based on the rules set on the AutoMod page.
A moderator asks about one link and gets: A moderator asks about one link and gets an answer back. None of this happens on its own — this is the half of Check Link you reach for when a link looks odd and you want a second opinion before clicking it.
Every link posted in chat is handed to t: Every link posted in chat is handed to the scanner in the background, before anybody has had the chance to click it. Nobody asks for these and nobody has to be watching. The Link Filter still applies its own rules to that link first — the scan is an extra safety check on top, not a replacement for it. Your exemptions apply to these scans too: the broadcaster, moderators, anyone on the excluded lists, and whichever of VIPs, subscribers and followers you have exempted are not scanned.

A different sentence depending on what was actually found, instead of one message for everything. Whichever fits is used when a message is deleted; leave one empty and it falls back to the Remove Message.

When several apply at once, the most explanatory one wins: disguised characters first, then advertising link, promo code, offer, wording, and bot mention last. Use {categories} if you want the message to name the others too.
What the Spam Learner reports back in ch: What the Spam Learner reports back in chat. {0}, {1} and {2} are positional and always mean keywords, phrases and TLDs, in that order; click a chip to drop one in at the cursor. All four messages stay silent while 'Reply In Chat' is off on the Spam Learner page.
Twitch Warn Message and Final Warn (Esca: Twitch Warn Message and Final Warn (Escalated) are shown on Twitch's warning screen, where only {count} is filled in. If 'Additional Reply In Chat' is on, the same text is also posted to chat — there {user}, {reason} and {duration} work as well.
Leave the two Chat Reply messages empty: Leave the two Chat Reply messages empty and the chat reply is the same text as the warning screen. Fill one in and it is used for the chat reply only, so you can put {user} in chat without it showing up as literal text on the warning screen.
Sent back by whisper when someone DMs th: Sent back by whisper when someone DMs the bot a link, rather than posted in chat. Neither whispered reply takes placeholders — they are whispered exactly as written.
Everything TwitchSentry knows about your: Everything TwitchSentry knows about your channel is a handful of files in one folder: your settings, the replies you have written, and what the Spam Learner has worked out from your chat. A backup is a dated copy of them, so a disk that gives up or a file that ends up half-written costs you a restore rather than an evening of setting it all up again. The other three areas, language files, logs and cache, are either re-downloaded on their own or a record of what happened rather than a setting you would have to write again; all five together are the whole TwitchSentry folder.
Only the parts that backup actually cont: Only the parts that backup actually contains are touched: restoring a settings-only backup leaves your logs and your learned spam data exactly where they are, and nothing is ever deleted. Before anything is restored, a copy of the current state is put aside in the same backup folder, so a restore you did not mean is itself undoable. The settings window reopens afterwards to show what was restored, and any unsaved changes in it are discarded.
What TwitchSentry has been saying about: What TwitchSentry has been saying about itself, out of the Streamer.bot log. Everything a module could not do - an API key that is still a placeholder, a download that failed, an action Twitch refused - is reported on the Status Log rather than in chat, so that is the page to open when something quietly did not happen.
Lets a chat message speak of a viewer by:
Lets a chat message speak of a viewer by the pronouns they set on pronouns.alejo.io. Put {pronoun:he|she|they} into the message, with the words your language needs: the first is used for he/him, the second for she/her, the third for they/them and for anyone whose pronouns are not known (none set, or this switch off). Other pronouns there, such as xe/xem, fae/faer or it/its, take the first form with the viewer's own words in place of he, him, his and himself. If the first form is not English, they take the third.
Example: {pronoun:He is|She is|They are} back in chat. For xe/xem: Xe is back in chat.

Twitch itself keeps no pronouns, so only viewers who set theirs there are known. Streamer.bot looks them up and remembers them.
The first form for he/him, the second fo: The first form for he/him, the second for she/her, the third for they/them and anyone whose pronouns are not known. Other pronouns such as xe/xem or it/its take the first form in their own words (He is → Xe is). Needs 'Use Viewer Pronouns' on General Settings.
Not in Streamer.bot's Commands tab under: Not in Streamer.bot's Commands tab under the id TwitchSentry knows them by, so nothing answers them: {list}. A command deleted and made again gets a new id - import the action set again.
Message Filter: 'Flood Repeat' is below: Message Filter: 'Flood Repeat' is below 3, so ordinary writing like 'hello' or '!!' counts as character spam, which can scare new viewers away. 3 or more is recommended.
Raid Protection: 'Flood Repeat Min' is b: Raid Protection: 'Flood Repeat Min' is below 3, so ordinary writing like 'hello' or '!!' counts as character spam and pushes a raid towards emote-only, which can scare the raiders away. 3 or more is recommended.

Add the triggers 'Twitch > Shield Mode Begin' and 'Twitch > Shield Mode End' to the RaidProtection or the FollowProtection action, or turn the automatic lift off.
